segments.resume: The narrator opens by claiming that Einstein was wrong about free will. Physicists tested reality with giant telescopes aimed 7.8 billion light-years away, and the result forces a choice: either space and time are illusions or every choice you make was decided before Earth existed.
segments.texte: You chose to click on this video. You thought it was your own free will. Even Albert Einstein would have agreed with you. Einstein was dead wrong. Quantum physicists pointed giant telescopes 7.8 billion light years into the deep cosmos to test the fabric of reality. What they found changes [music] everything. Either space and time are complete illusions or your entire life is scripted. Every thought you've ever had and every choice you'll make was already decided long before Earth even existed.

segments.titre: Einstein, relativité générale et réalisme local
segments.resume: Einstein's general relativity describes space and time as a woven 4D fabric in which reality is logical and predictable. His belief in local realism has two parts: things exist whether or not they are observed, and an event cannot instantly affect something far away without a link, delay or signal.
segments.texte: Albert Einstein's greatest gift to the world was the theory of general relativity, also known as Einstein's theory of gravity. He discovered that space and time are woven together like a giant invisible 4D fabric. According to Einstein, reality is predictable, logical, and it makes total sense. He believed in the concept of local realism and it boiled down to two simple concepts. Things are real [music] whether you're looking at them or not. A rock on Mars doesn't stop existing because no one is there to see it. And events occurring in one location can't instantly affect something happening millions of miles away. There has to be a link, a delay, or a signal. It's a common sense view of the physical world, something even the average person can generally understand.

segments.titre: La physique quantique et l'intrication contre le réalisme local
segments.resume: Quantum physics found that unobserved particles dissolve into mathematical probabilities rather than sitting in one place. Quantum entanglement links particles across any distance so that spinning one instantly affects the other, which broke Einstein's rule that nothing travels faster than light.
segments.texte: Then quantum physics completely shattered what Einstein believed in. When scientists started looking at reality on a subatomic level, they made discoveries that turned the entire concept of local realism on its head. They found that instead of existing in a specific location, unobserved particles dissolved into a ghostly mathematical probabilities. And it gets weirder. Digging deeper, they developed the theory of quantum entanglement. Essentially, it means that two or more tiny particles can become linked even if they're in completely different places. Like putting one at the North Pole and the other on the moon, they still mirror one another. >> [music] >> Spin one and the other will spin. This happens instantly without delay. For Einstein, that was ridiculous. It broke his rule that nothing could travel faster than light.

segments.titre: Einstein rejette l'intrication : action fantomatique et variables cachées
segments.resume: Einstein mocked quantum theory and called entanglement spooky action at a distance, going to his grave convinced quantum physics was flawed. He believed particles carried a hidden variable set at birth, so they simply followed a script rather than communicating across light-years.
segments.texte: He famously mocked colleagues stating, "Do you really believe the moon is not there when you're not looking at it?" He jokingly called quantum entanglement "spooky [music] action at a distance." He went to his grave believing that quantum physics was fundamentally flawed. Einstein believed scientists were missing a secret variable, like some sort of special property that was built into particles at their birth, which dictated their behavior in the future. To him, the particles weren't communicating across light-years, they were just following a script that we couldn't read yet.

segments.titre: Le débat et le test proposé par John Bell dans les années 1960
segments.resume: For decades quantum theory was dismissed as philosophy and journals refused such papers. In the 1960s Northern Irish physicist John Stewart Bell proposed a test with a limit on how synchronized separate particles could be, which would show whether Einstein or the quantum physicists were right.
segments.texte: For decades, scientists argued [music] both sides of the debate. For a long time, quantum theories were dismissed as philosophy or even crackpottery. Many scientific journals literally refused to publish papers on the topic. >> [music] >> Aspiring quantum students were encouraged to stick to classical physics instead. And then, in the 1960s, something changed. A Northern Irish physicist called John Stewart Bell proposed [music] a test that could potentially settle the spooky action debate once and for all. It would determine whether distant entangled particles [music] communicate instantly or if Einstein was right all along. If Einstein was right, well, there had to be some sort of limit on how synchronized two separate particles [music] could be. If the quantum physicists were right, however, they would smash through that limit.

segments.titre: Les premières expériences de Clauser, Freedman et Aspect
segments.resume: Bell lacked the technology to run his experiment, which only became possible in the 1970s and 80s through John Clauser, Stuart Freedman and Alain Aspect. The particles broke Bell's mathematical limit every time, showing that entanglement is real.
segments.texte: But Bell couldn't actually perform the experiment, the technology [music] didn't exist. It wasn't until the 1970s and '80s that a new generation of scientists, such as John Clauser, Stuart Freedman, and Alain Aspect, were able to put Bell's theorem to the test. [music] And Einstein lost every time. The particles shattered Bell's mathematical limit, proving quantum entanglement was real.

segments.titre: Les failles de détection et de localité
segments.resume: Einstein's defenders argued the experiments had loopholes. The detection loophole claimed equipment missed particles and scientists cherry-picked pairs, while the locality loophole claimed particles could exchange a fast hidden signal before measurement. Faster electronics and more efficient detectors gradually closed both.
segments.texte: But Einstein's acolytes refused to back down. [music] They claimed the experiments were rigged or pointed out massive loopholes in the logic. First, there was the detection or fair sampling loophole. Skeptics argued that existing scientific equipment simply wasn't accurate and reliable enough to capture every particle. They accused scientists of inadvertently cherry-picking the pairs that lined up with their hypothesis. And then there was the locality loophole. This argued that the particles were communicating just like [music] Einstein thought, just using a hidden signal that moved incredibly fast. If the particles had a microsecond to send messages before being captured, then the whole test was invalid. >> [music] >> As the years went by and technology improved, scientists found ways to shut down these loopholes. They built ultra-fast electronic systems to counter the locality loophole argument, and they made detectors more efficient to collect [music] broader and more reliable measurements.

segments.titre: Le premier test de Bell sans faille en 2015 et les cinq sigma
segments.resume: In 2015 scientists achieved the first loophole-free Bell test and Einstein lost again. Five sigma is the gold standard in statistics, reached by the Higgs boson discovery at CERN, while the Bell test hit 11.5 sigma, making chance practically impossible.
segments.texte: By 2015, they had achieved the holy grail of quantum physics, the first loophole-free Bell test. And again, Einstein lost. The data was overwhelming. In statistics, a discovery is confirmed at a level called five sigma. It is the gold standard. When it hits that, there's an almost unimaginably microscopic probability that the results were just random chance. The discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN achieved five sigma. The 2015 Bell test hit 11.5. The odds of that happening by chance are practically zero. It is more likely that you win the lottery every week for the rest of your life. The science was indisputable, but Einstein's defenders did dispute it. They had one more card to play.

segments.titre: La faille du libre arbitre (freedom of choice)
segments.resume: The last loophole is freedom of choice: Bell tests assume scientists can pick detector settings freely, but a hidden thread could link the settings and the particle, making entanglement look real when it was predetermined. Since any link could date back millions of years, the loophole seems impossible to close unless the experiment leaves Earth.
segments.texte: They pointed to the last but significant loophole, the freedom of choice or free will loophole, the most complex loophole of all. In a typical Bell test, scientists fire a pair of entangled photons toward two separate detectors. To keep the tests fair, the detectors must randomly switch their measuring filters at the very last millisecond before the particles arrive. The free will loophole argument states that the tests like these operate on the assumption that the scientists have freedom of choice to pick whatever setting they want. They aren't influenced into making one decision over another. But what if they don't? What if there is some unknown hidden thread connecting the machine setting and the particle being measured? It might look like quantum entanglement, but it's actually proof of some sort of secret predetermined link between the two. The question the machine asks and the answer the particle gives were rigged from the start. The loophole is practically impossible to close. People can easily claim that there's some sort of connection between the microchips inside lab computers and the particles in the air around them. A connection that potentially dates back millions of years. Unless you can break that connection, you can never prove Einstein wrong.

segments.titre: Le Bell test cosmique de 2018 aux îles Canaries
segments.resume: In 2018 a team led by Nobel laureate Anton Zeilinger, with physicists from MIT and UC San Diego, gathered at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory on La Palma. They set up two large telescopes and a laser producing entangled photon pairs, planning to choose detector settings using the universe itself instead of a computer or human.
segments.texte: So, in 2018, a team of scientists decided to do the unthinkable. To close the loophole, they had to escape Earth and take their experiment deep into the cosmos. Led by Nobel laureate Dr. Anton Zeilinger, the team made up of theoretical physicists from MIT and UC San Diego gathered at the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory on La Palma in the Canary Islands. Their mission, [music] a cosmic Bell test. They set up two enormous astronomical telescopes, one measuring 11.8 ft across and the other 13.7 ft. They also had an advanced laser system that generated entangled pairs of photons before firing one of each pair toward each telescope site. There was one thing that made this experiment so different. To choose the detector settings, they didn't use a computer or a human. They used the universe itself.

segments.titre: Des quasars lointains comme générateur aléatoire
segments.resume: The telescopes pointed at two quasars, one 7.8 billion and the other 12.2 billion light-years away, and the color fluctuations of their ancient light set the detector settings. These quasars could not have communicated, so the universe acted as the ultimate random number generator and the free will loophole should have been shut.
segments.texte: The team pointed their telescopes into the deepest recesses of space toward two extremely far away galactic cores called quasars. These were not local stars or even nearby galaxies. One quasar was 7.8 billion light-years away. The other was even further, 12.2 billion light-years. That means the light from these two galaxy cores had been traveling through the void for [music] billions of years just to get to the Earth. And that made it the perfect tool to slam the free will loophole shut once and for all. The strategy was brilliant. As the ancient light from the quasars entered the telescope sites, >> [music] >> scientists captured the random color fluctuations. That was converted into numerical signals, which were then used to change the detector settings right as the entangled photons arrived. The universe became the ultimate cosmic random number generator. The quasars were so old, so far apart, and so far away from the Earth they had no way of communicating with each other. If Einstein was right, any measurable correlations between the photons should have flattened out the quantum effects. The experiment should have failed.

segments.titre: Résultat : la mécanique quantique gagne encore
segments.resume: The entangled photons still behaved as if connected through space and time, even when the choices came from light that left its source billions of years ago. Quantum mechanics won again and the result was not close.
segments.texte: That's not what happened. When the scientists analyzed their findings, their conclusions were unequivocal. Just like in so many other Bell tests, the entangled photons behaved like they were connected through space and time. Even when the choices were dictated by light that left its source billions of years ago, nothing changed. Quantum mechanics won again, and it wasn't even close.

segments.titre: Une chance sur cent milliards de milliards et la dernière carte : le superdéterminisme
segments.resume: Alan Guth said the odds the result was a fluke were 1 in 100 billion billion, illustrated by repeatedly picking the same grain of sand on a beach. The experiment shows common sense reality is dead, and the only card left for Einstein's side is superdeterminism.
segments.texte: Dr. Alan Guth revealed the possibility of the test results being a fluke were 1 in 100 billion billion. To put that into perspective, imagine going to a beach, picking up a single grain of sand, and then dropping it among the trillion other grains. And then you close your eyes and you immediately pick up that same grain of sand over and over again. That's a statistical impossibility. That's what made this experiment matter so much. It proved beyond a shadow of a doubt that our common sense view of reality is dead. If anyone wants to hold on to Einstein's theory, they can't blame faulty equipment or a local lab condition. The only card that they have left to play is a concept so mind-bending it sounds insane. Superdeterminism. >> [music] >>

segments.titre: Le superdéterminisme : un univers écrit depuis le Big Bang
segments.resume: Science relies on statistical independence, meaning a particle does not know in advance how it will be measured, and superdeterminism denies this. If true, the quasars followed a script written at the Big Bang that matches the photons in a Canary Islands lab, so experiments are illusions, nothing is random and humans have no free will, like actors reading lines or trains on tracks.
segments.texte: To understand how terrifying this is, you have to understand how science works. In normal scientific circles, we rely on something called statistical independence. [music] It means that when a scientist flicks a switch to measure a particle, the particle doesn't know that the switch is about to be flicked. Superdeterminism says [music] that is a lie. It argues that everything in the universe has been locked in since the dawn of time. So, if superdeterminism is accurate, those distant quasars weren't as random as they seemed to be. Instead, [music] they were reading from a script that was written billions of years ago during the Big Bang. A cosmic script that [music] those two exact quasars would emit a specific type of light in a particular way that would perfectly match the subatomic states of photons generated in a Canary Islands lab. Under this rule, there is no such thing as an independent experiment. Experiments in science are little more than an illusion. Everything we do, everything we measure, every tool we use is already predetermined. That means humans don't have any agency of any kind. There's no free will, nothing is random, every single thing that's ever happened and ever will happen was always going to happen that exact same way. And there's nothing we could do to change it. We're all just going through the motions like trains following tracks or actors reading lines that were written well before they were born.

segments.titre: Bell reconnaît l'échappatoire déterministe
segments.resume: John Stewart Bell told the BBC in the 1980s that the only way to avoid faster-than-light signals is absolute determinism with no free will, since the universe already knows every measurement outcome. He thought it implausible and most physicists dismissed it as a cop-out, yet quantum progress is pushing scientists toward a choice between two worldviews.
segments.texte: John Stewart Bell even acknowledged this argument back in the 1980s telling the BBC, "There's a way to escape the inference of superluminal speeds and spooky action, but it involves absolute determinism, the complete absence of free will. There is no need for a faster than light signal to tell particle A what measurement has been carried out on particle B because the universe already knows what that measurement and its outcome will be." Bell also stated that he believed this concept to be implausible. Most physicists flat-out ignored that saying that that was a cop-out that could never be tested or proven. But as quantum physics has evolved, scientists are being backed into a corner. They're being increasingly forced to face up to the idea of superdeterminism and that leads them to choose between two very different views of the world.

segments.titre: Le choix : superdéterminisme ou réalisme local réfuté
segments.resume: Either superdeterminism is real and the universe is hard-coded, or local realism is disproven and distant particles can influence each other faster than light. Most scientists choose the second option because accepting predetermination would make science pointless, but it implies most of what we know about space and time is wrong.
segments.texte: Either superdeterminism is real and that [music] means the whole universe is hard-coded and independent agency is an illusion, or that Einstein was wrong. Local realism has been disproven and particles even in completely different places can remain connected and directly influence one another at faster-than-light speeds. Most scientists [music] stopped for the second option because the idea of accepting superdeterminism doesn't sit right with them. If you accept that everything is predetermined, then scientific pursuits aren't worth pursuing at all. But if local realism is wrong, then so is most of what we know about space and time.

segments.titre: De l'espace-temps de Newton et Einstein à un espace-temps qui n'est pas réel
segments.resume: Newton saw space as a rigid stage and Einstein wove space and time into a 4D fabric, but both treated it as a backdrop for reality. The cosmic Bell test suggests distance is meaningless for entangled particles, so physical space is not what we think and space-time may not be real.
segments.texte: Isaac Newton famously saw space as a kind of rigid empty arena or a stage. Einstein took that idea to a new level suggesting that space and time weave around one another into a complex 4D fabric called space-time. But even in Einstein's vision, space-time was still seen as a kind of backdrop to reality. It was a physical layer that dictated where objects were, how quickly they can move, and how cause and effect worked together. The cosmic bell test shattered all of that. By closing that last loophole, the Canary Islands research team forced scientists across the globe to confront a whole new type of reality. A reality in which distance is meaningless. A reality in which particle A on the Earth can impact particle B on Jupiter instantly. If physical distance doesn't matter to entangled particles, then physical [music] space is not what we think it is. Einstein's space-time fabric clashes with quantum mechanics. That suggests something deeply unsettling. Space-time isn't [music] real. We may perceive it as real, but that's just a flaw in human nature.

segments.titre: Analogie de la chaleur : l'espace-temps comme phénomène émergent
segments.resume: Heat in hot water feels real, yet a single molecule only has kinetic energy, so heat emerges from many colliding molecules. Theoretical physicists apply the same logic to space-time, saying it is a byproduct emerging from a vast network of entangled quantum particles exchanging information.
segments.texte: If you pour boiling water into a cup and you touch it, it feels hot. You'll notice a rise in temperature. But if you zoom in and you look at an individual molecule of water, it does not have an increase in temperature. It just has an increase in kinetic energy. It is moving fast. The heat you feel is a byproduct of large amounts of energy across large amounts of molecules, all interacting and colliding with one another. It's real to us because we can feel it in our fingertips. But on a subatomic level, it's not real. And today's theoretical physicists are taking that logic and applying it to space and time. Space-time, they say, is not a stage or a fabric. It's closer to a byproduct. Just as heat emerges from the chaotic motion of molecules, physical space and time emerges from the unimaginably vast network of entangled quantum particles constantly swapping information.

segments.titre: Le principe holographique et la réalité 3D projetée
segments.resume: The holographic principle proposes that our 3D reality is a projection from a 2D screen at the edge of the cosmos, where there is no gravity or spatial distance, only interacting quantum bits. It is compared to a 3D movie that looks deep but is flat when you touch the screen.
segments.texte: And as theoretical physicists slowly turn away from Einstein's teachings, they've had to to up with an alternative way to visualize the universe, the holographic principle or holographic universe. This theory suggests that our 3D reality is actually a kind of projection emanating from the vast 2D screen that sits at the edge of the cosmos. On that screen, there's no such thing as gravity, spatial distance, or 3D space. It's just a collection of quantum bits all interacting with each other to project our reality into existence. It's almost like when you watch a movie in 3D, it might look and feel as though the objects are moving toward you, but if you stand up and touch the screen, everything is flat.

segments.titre: L'holographie explique l'action fantomatique et l'illusion du temps
segments.resume: On a flat 2D screen, entangled particles are not really far apart, so spooky action at a distance needs no magical communication. The same logic suggests that time as past, present and future is an illusion produced by our brains misreading quantum data.
segments.texte: The holographic principle actually explains Einstein's spooky action at a distance idea well. If the two particles are entangled on a flat 2D screen, they're not actually communicating with one another in some magical mysterious way across light-years of 3D space. We just perceive them as being far apart, but in reality, they aren't. That same sort of logic can also be applied to time. We experience it in a linear sequential format, past, present, and future, but that too might just be an illusion. It's our brain's desperate attempt to interpret complex quantum data unfolding on a flat plane that we're hardwired to misunderstand.

segments.titre: Le dilemme terrifiant : libre arbitre ou espace-temps
segments.resume: The cosmic Bell test forces a dilemma: accept superdeterminism, where space and time may be real but free will is fake, or reject it and accept that space and time are a holographic projection of quantum data. Either way one fundamental belief about the world, life or choices is wrong.
segments.texte: Even if you want to reject these ideas, the alternative is not any more comforting. The cosmic bell test has plunged humanity into a terrifying dilemma. On the one hand, you can believe in superdeterminism, and that means that space and time as we know them might be real, but free will is fake and nothing you do is ever really your decision. On the other hand, you can reject superdeterminism, but then you have to accept that space and time are simply illusions. The world around you is basically a holographic movie projection of quantum data. Either way, you have to accept that at least one of those fundamental things you thought about the world, about your life, and about your own choices and experiences is wrong, and that is the most frightening part of all.

segments.titre: La panspermie et la météorite martienne
segments.resume: Panspermia is the theory that life spreads between planets on asteroids and comets. A Martian meteorite found in Antarctica may hold fossilized microorganisms, and it was probably launched from Mars by an asteroid impact, so we might all be Martians.

segments.titre: Les tardigrades survivent dans l'espace

segments.titre: Histoire de l'idée des trous noirs : Michell, Einstein, Cygnus X-1
segments.resume: English clergyman John Michell first proposed black holes in November 1784 and noted they could be detected by their gravitational effects. Einstein's general relativity showed they could form, yet he doubted they existed in nature, until Cygnus X-1 became the first observed black hole in 1972.
segments.texte: Eight, the first theory positing the existence of black holes was from an English clergyman named John Michell in November 1784. Seven, despite proving through general relativity that black holes could form, Einstein himself did not believe they could form in the natural world. segments.titre: Preuves observationnelles des trous noirs : Voie lactée, Gezari, ondes gravitationnelles
segments.resume: In 2002 astronomers presented evidence of a supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. In 2012 Suvi Gezari's team captured the first visual evidence of one swallowing a red giant, and in 2015 gravitational waves from two merging black holes were detected.
